[smarts.bio] The tools above each run ONE step. Multi-step work — de-novo protein and nanobody design, variant calling, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq — runs as a pipeline, listed separately via smarts_list_pipelines:
  quality-control — FastQC + MultiQC report generation for one or more sequencing datasets.
  alignment-wes — Whole-exome sequencing alignment: FastQC → Trimmomatic → BWA-MEM → Picard → GATK BQSR.
  whole-genome-sequencing — WGS alignment with QC, duplicate marking, and variant-ready BAM generation.
  rna-seq-analysis — FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → SAMtools → featureCounts → DESeq2.
  atac-seq — Adapter trimming → Bowtie2 alignment → MACS2 peak calling → fragment size analysis.
  chip-seq — ChIP-seq alignment, MACS2 peak calling, and de novo motif enrichment with HOMER.
  gatk-variant-calling — Germline SNP & indel discovery using GATK4 HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode.
  somatic-variant-calling — Tumor-normal somatic SNV & indel detection using GATK Mutect2 with artifact filtering.
  protein-binder-design-validated — AI binder design (generative models) + automated binding affinity validation with Boltz-2.
  nanobody-discovery — De novo VHH nanobody design: RFdiffusion3 holds a real VHH framework fixed and diffuses only CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 against the epitope, ProteinMPNN designs sequences, RoseTTAFold3 validates, then Boltz-2 co-folds each candidate with the antigen and ranks by interface confidence (ipTM, pTM, pLDDT).
  enzyme-engineering — Redesigns an enzyme scaffold with its catalytic residues held fixed, validates the fold with Boltz-2, and scores thermostability with ThermoMPNN.
  structure-based-drug-discovery — Target structure retrieval or prediction, binding site identification, and virtual screening.
If the task needs generation, alignment-then-calling, or several tools in order, inspect a pipeline with smarts_get_pipeline before running single tools.

[smarts.bio] The tools above each run ONE step. Multi-step work — de-novo protein and nanobody design, variant calling, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq — runs as a pipeline, listed separately via smarts_list_pipelines:
  quality-control — FastQC + MultiQC report generation for one or more sequencing datasets.
  alignment-wes — Whole-exome sequencing alignment: FastQC → Trimmomatic → BWA-MEM → Picard → GATK BQSR.
  whole-genome-sequencing — WGS alignment with QC, duplicate marking, and variant-ready BAM generation.
  rna-seq-analysis — FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → SAMtools → featureCounts → DESeq2.
  atac-seq — Adapter trimming → Bowtie2 alignment → MACS2 peak calling → fragment size analysis.
  chip-seq — ChIP-seq alignment, MACS2 peak calling, and de novo motif enrichment with HOMER.
  gatk-variant-calling — Germline SNP & indel discovery using GATK4 HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode.
  somatic-variant-calling — Tumor-normal somatic SNV & indel detection using GATK Mutect2 with artifact filtering.
  protein-binder-design-validated — AI binder design (generative models) + automated binding affinity validation with Boltz-2.
  nanobody-discovery — De novo VHH nanobody design: RFdiffusion3 holds a real VHH framework fixed and diffuses only CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 against the epitope, ProteinMPNN designs sequences, RoseTTAFold3 validates, then Boltz-2 co-folds each candidate with the antigen and ranks by interface confidence (ipTM, pTM, pLDDT).
  enzyme-engineering — Redesigns an enzyme scaffold with its catalytic residues held fixed, validates the fold with Boltz-2, and scores thermostability with ThermoMPNN.
  structure-based-drug-discovery — Target structure retrieval or prediction, binding site identification, and virtual screening.
If the task needs generation, alignment-then-calling, or several tools in order, inspect a pipeline with smarts_get_pipeline before running single tools.

[smarts.bio] The tools above each run ONE step. Multi-step work — de-novo protein and nanobody design, variant calling, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq — runs as a pipeline, listed separately via smarts_list_pipelines:
  quality-control — FastQC + MultiQC report generation for one or more sequencing datasets.
  alignment-wes — Whole-exome sequencing alignment: FastQC → Trimmomatic → BWA-MEM → Picard → GATK BQSR.
  whole-genome-sequencing — WGS alignment with QC, duplicate marking, and variant-ready BAM generation.
  rna-seq-analysis — FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → SAMtools → featureCounts → DESeq2.
  atac-seq — Adapter trimming → Bowtie2 alignment → MACS2 peak calling → fragment size analysis.
  chip-seq — ChIP-seq alignment, MACS2 peak calling, and de novo motif enrichment with HOMER.
  gatk-variant-calling — Germline SNP & indel discovery using GATK4 HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode.
  somatic-variant-calling — Tumor-normal somatic SNV & indel detection using GATK Mutect2 with artifact filtering.
  protein-binder-design-validated — AI binder design (generative models) + automated binding affinity validation with Boltz-2.
  nanobody-discovery — De novo VHH nanobody design: RFdiffusion3 holds a real VHH framework fixed and diffuses only CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 against the epitope, ProteinMPNN designs sequences, RoseTTAFold3 validates, then Boltz-2 co-folds each candidate with the antigen and ranks by interface confidence (ipTM, pTM, pLDDT).
  enzyme-engineering — Redesigns an enzyme scaffold with its catalytic residues held fixed, validates the fold with Boltz-2, and scores thermostability with ThermoMPNN.
  structure-based-drug-discovery — Target structure retrieval or prediction, binding site identification, and virtual screening.
If the task needs generation, alignment-then-calling, or several tools in order, inspect a pipeline with smarts_get_pipeline before running single tools.

[smarts.bio] The tools above each run ONE step. Multi-step work — de-novo protein and nanobody design, variant calling, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq — runs as a pipeline, listed separately via smarts_list_pipelines:
  quality-control — FastQC + MultiQC report generation for one or more sequencing datasets.
  alignment-wes — Whole-exome sequencing alignment: FastQC → Trimmomatic → BWA-MEM → Picard → GATK BQSR.
  whole-genome-sequencing — WGS alignment with QC, duplicate marking, and variant-ready BAM generation.
  rna-seq-analysis — FastQC → Trimmomatic → HISAT2 → SAMtools → featureCounts → DESeq2.
  atac-seq — Adapter trimming → Bowtie2 alignment → MACS2 peak calling → fragment size analysis.
  chip-seq — ChIP-seq alignment, MACS2 peak calling, and de novo motif enrichment with HOMER.
  gatk-variant-calling — Germline SNP & indel discovery using GATK4 HaplotypeCaller in GVCF mode.
  somatic-variant-calling — Tumor-normal somatic SNV & indel detection using GATK Mutect2 with artifact filtering.
  protein-binder-design-validated — AI binder design (generative models) + automated binding affinity validation with Boltz-2.
  nanobody-discovery — De novo VHH nanobody design: RFdiffusion3 holds a real VHH framework fixed and diffuses only CDR1/CDR2/CDR3 against the epitope, ProteinMPNN designs sequences, RoseTTAFold3 validates, then Boltz-2 co-folds each candidate with the antigen and ranks by interface confidence (ipTM, pTM, pLDDT).
  enzyme-engineering — Redesigns an enzyme scaffold with its catalytic residues held fixed, validates the fold with Boltz-2, and scores thermostability with ThermoMPNN.
  structure-based-drug-discovery — Target structure retrieval or prediction, binding site identification, and virtual screening.
If the task needs generation, alignment-then-calling, or several tools in order, inspect a pipeline with smarts_get_pipeline before running single tools.

content.text:
The design job is submitted and running. Here's the design and its rationale.

## Design strategy

A nanobody (VHH) is a single ~13 kDa immunoglobulin domain: four framework regions (FR1–FR4) forming the β-sandwich, with three CDR loops carrying essentially all the specificity. So the design problem is **hold the framework, rebuild the CDRs against a chosen epitope** — which is exactly what the platform's `nanobody-discovery` pipeline does (RFdiffusion3 CDR diffusion → ProteinMPNN sequence design → RoseTTAFold3 validation → Boltz-2 co-folding with the antigen).

**Target — PDB 1DPX.** Confirmed via `pdb-toolkit` (operation `metadata`): "Structure of Hen Egg-White Lysozyme", X-ray, **1.65 Å**, R-work 0.187 / R-free 0.246, space group P4₃2₁2, Weiss, Palm & Hilgenfeld. Single polymer entity, 129 residues. Good resolution and a monomeric single chain — a clean design target.

**Epitope — the active-site cleft (hotspots 35, 52, 62, 63, 101, 108).** I chose this deliberately rather than letting the binding site drift:

- It is the single largest concave feature on an otherwise fairly smooth, compact globular protein. Nanobodies have a strong, well-documented preference for cleft and cavity epitopes — their long CDR3 and convex paratope insert where a flat two-chain Fv paratope cannot. Targeting the cleft plays to the format's strength.
- A nanobody bound here is **functionally blocking**, not just binding — it should inhibit glycoside-hydrolase activity (EC 3.2.1.17), which makes the design testable by a simple lysozyme activity assay rather than only by biophysics.
- This is the validated precedent epitope: cAb-Lys3 binds HEL by inserting CDR3 into the substrate cleft.

The hotspot numbering is grounded, not assumed. UniProt **P00698** (LYSC_CHICK) annotates the catalytic dyad at precursor positions **53** and **70**, plus a substrate-binding site at **119**. The signal peptide is residues 1–18 and the mature chain is 19–147, so PDB numbering = precursor − 18, giving **Glu35**, **Asp52**, **Asp101**. I then indexed the mature 129-residue sequence to confirm each hotspot identity: E35, D52, Q57, W62, W63, D101, A107, W108. I passed the six that line the cleft floor and walls — the catalytic dyad (35, 52), the Trp62/Trp63 pair that forms the hydrophobic sugar-binding subsites, and Asp101/Trp108 at the far end.

**Framework — 1MEL (cAb-Lys3).** Confirmed via `pdb-toolkit`: "Crystal structure of a camel single-domain VH antibody fragment in complex with lysozyme", X-ray 2.5 Å, Desmyter, Transue & Arbabi Gharoudi. The pipeline keeps only FR1–FR4 and discards its CDRs. I picked it because it is a genuine camelid VHH known to fold and crystallize well while supporting an unusually long cleft-penetrating CDR3 — the framework geometry is proven compatible with this exact epitope.

**One caveat you should weigh, since the framework is a developability decision and the pipeline deliberately has no default:** 1MEL's framework comes from an anti-lysozyme nanobody. That is helpful for the structural question but makes this a less clean test of *de novo* design, and a llama/camel framework is not a therapeutic starting point. If you want a stricter benchmark, rerun with a naive framework unrelated to lysozyme (e.g. NbBcII10, an anti-β-lactamase VHH) and compare ipTM. If you want a therapeutic lead, start from a humanized framework instead. Both are a one-parameter change; say the word and I'll launch either alongside this run.

**CDR3 length 16–22, 8 designs.** VHH CDR3s run long (12–24); 16–22 biases toward loops long enough to actually reach into the cleft rather than cap it. Eight candidates is near the pipeline's maximum of 10, giving diversity to rank.

## Design strategy

A nanobody (VHH) is a single ~13 kDa immunoglobulin domain: four framework regions (FR1–FR4) forming the β-sandwich, with three CDR loops carrying essentially all the specificity. So the design problem is **hold the framework, rebuild the CDRs against a chosen epitope** — which is exactly what the platform's `nanobody-discovery` pipeline does (RFdiffusion3 CDR diffusion → ProteinMPNN sequence design → RoseTTAFold3 validation → Boltz-2 co-folding with the antigen).

**Target — PDB 1DPX.** Confirmed via `pdb-toolkit` (operation `metadata`): "Structure of Hen Egg-White Lysozyme", X-ray, **1.65 Å**, R-work 0.187 / R-free 0.246, space group P4₃2₁2, Weiss, Palm & Hilgenfeld. Single polymer entity, 129 residues. Good resolution and a monomeric single chain — a clean design target.

**Epitope — the active-site cleft (hotspots 35, 52, 62, 63, 101, 108).** I chose this deliberately rather than letting the binding site drift:

- It is the single largest concave feature on an otherwise fairly smooth, compact globular protein. Nanobodies have a strong, well-documented preference for cleft and cavity epitopes — their long CDR3 and convex paratope insert where a flat two-chain Fv paratope cannot. Targeting the cleft plays to the format's strength.
- A nanobody bound here is **functionally blocking**, not just binding — it should inhibit glycoside-hydrolase activity (EC 3.2.1.17), which makes the design testable by a simple lysozyme activity assay rather than only by biophysics.
- This is the validated precedent epitope: cAb-Lys3 binds HEL by inserting CDR3 into the substrate cleft.

The hotspot numbering is grounded, not assumed. UniProt **P00698** (LYSC_CHICK) annotates the catalytic dyad at precursor positions **53** and **70**, plus a substrate-binding site at **119**. The signal peptide is residues 1–18 and the mature chain is 19–147, so PDB numbering = precursor − 18, giving **Glu35**, **Asp52**, **Asp101**. I then indexed the mature 129-residue sequence to confirm each hotspot identity: E35, D52, Q57, W62, W63, D101, A107, W108. I passed the six that line the cleft floor and walls — the catalytic dyad (35, 52), the Trp62/Trp63 pair that forms the hydrophobic sugar-binding subsites, and Asp101/Trp108 at the far end.

**Framework — 1MEL (cAb-Lys3).** Confirmed via `pdb-toolkit`: "Crystal structure of a camel single-domain VH antibody fragment in complex with lysozyme", X-ray 2.5 Å, Desmyter, Transue & Arbabi Gharoudi. The pipeline keeps only FR1–FR4 and discards its CDRs. I picked it because it is a genuine camelid VHH known to fold and crystallize well while supporting an unusually long cleft-penetrating CDR3 — the framework geometry is proven compatible with this exact epitope.

**One caveat you should weigh, since the framework is a developability decision and the pipeline deliberately has no default:** 1MEL's framework comes from an anti-lysozyme nanobody. That is helpful for the structural question but makes this a less clean test of *de novo* design, and a llama/camel framework is not a therapeutic starting point. If you want a stricter benchmark, rerun with a naive framework unrelated to lysozyme (e.g. NbBcII10, an anti-β-lactamase VHH) and compare ipTM. If you want a therapeutic lead, start from a humanized framework instead. Both are a one-parameter change; say the word and I'll launch either alongside this run.

**CDR3 length 16–22, 8 designs.** VHH CDR3s run long (12–24); 16–22 biases toward loops long enough to actually reach into the cleft rather than cap it. Eight candidates is near the pipeline's maximum of 10, giving diversity to rank.

The run completed at **18:42:37 UTC on 2026-11-12**, duration **67.4 minutes** (4,044,583 ms), both steps `completed`. Results below are read directly from the output files in `pipelines/2026-11-12_17-35-13/`.

## What was produced

RFdiffusion3 generated 8 backbones (`rfd3_summary.json`: `num_designs: 8`), but ProteinMPNN emitted **10** sequences from them and Boltz-2 scored all 10 — so you have 10 candidates, not the 8 I requested.

Every design is **122 aa**, with FR1/FR2/FR3/FR4 at **100.0% identity** to the 1MEL framework (`vhh_annotation.json`) and the canonical Cys21–Cys95 disulfide intact in all 10. The framework was held fixed as intended; these are genuine VHH domains, not generic 122-residue binders.

## Ranking (Boltz-2 co-fold with HEL, `boltz2_summary.json`)

Ranked by **ipTM**. Mean pLDDT across the 10 complexes 88.49, mean pTM 0.878.

| Rank | Design | ipTM | pTM | pLDDT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | design_seq_2 | **0.877** | 0.931 | 89.65 |
| 2 | design_seq_10 | 0.845 | 0.903 | 87.11 |
| 3 | design_seq_4 | 0.796 | 0.889 | 89.06 |
| 4 | design_seq_3 | 0.792 | 0.887 | 91.46 |
| 5 | design_seq_6 | 0.787 | 0.882 | 84.82 |
| 6 | design_seq_8 | 0.783 | 0.867 | 88.22 |
| 7 | design_seq_7 | 0.765 | 0.875 | 90.14 |
| 8 | design_seq_5 | 0.759 | 0.871 | 89.03 |
| 9 | design_seq_1 | 0.752 | 0.827 | 88.11 |
| 10 | design_seq_9 | 0.707 | 0.846 | 87.26 |

**Top candidate — design_seq_2** (VHH chain; the co-folded file also contains HEL as chain B):

```
VQLQASGGGSVQAGGSLRLSCAASGADPPPSRLGWFRQAPGKEREGVASINTATGETYYADS
VKGRFTISQDNAKNTVYLLMNSLEPEDTAIYYCYAEQAGNGSSTLTVTHWGQGTQVTVSS
```
CDR1 `GADPPPSRLG` (25–34) · CDR2 `SINTATGET` (49–57) · CDR3 `YAEQAGNGSSTLTVTH` (96–111) · estimated pI 4.93 · structure `binding-affinity-prediction/boltz2/design_seq_2.cif`

As predicted, **no Kd or ΔG was produced** — `boltz2_summary.json` reports `affinity_computed: false` despite `affinity_requested: true`, exactly the protein–protein limitation the pipeline documents. ipTM is the only binding signal here.

## Four things that qualify this result

**1. There is no single winner.** The tool's own `ranking_note` says differences below ~0.09 ipTM are within Boltz-2 sampling noise, and flags designs 2, 10, 4, 3 and 6 as a **joint top band**. Treat those five as equivalent and test them in parallel rather than committing to design_seq_2.

**2. The 10 designs are one family, not 10 independent solutions.** Every CDR3 shares the core motif `AGNG(S/N)ST`; CDR2 is `SINTATG` + 2 residues in all 10; CDR1 is a `G/D-A-D/E-P-G/P-P-S` variant throughout. The diversity you'd normally want from 10 designs isn't there — the sampling converged.
